newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - Nedlloyd tumbles 20 percent on results.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Nedlloyd tumbles 20 percent on results.

text.p: Shares in Dutch shipping and road transport group Nedlloyd plunged 20 percent on Thursday after it announced a 54 percent slide in 1996 net profit and declined to give a profits forecast.
At the close of trading, Nedlloyd shares were down 11.50 guilders at 45.50 in a sharply weaker Amsterdam market, rattled by fears of a rate rise in U.S. interest rates.
Koninklijke Nedlloyd Groep's net profit after extraordinary items amounted to 49 million guilders ($26 million) in 1996 against 106 million in 1995. It gave no profit forecast.

"We make no statement on the outlook. It is too early in the year. It is also too early in the (P&O Nedlloyd container) merger process. 1997 is a transition year," chairman Leo Berndsen told a news conference.
The 1996 result was marred by the inclusion in the 1995 result of net extraordinary gains of 29 million guilders. There were no such non-recurring items in 1996.
The dividend of 1.25 guilders per share was unchanged.

Despite an improved second half, ocean shipping operating profits more than halved to 25 million guilders from 57 million in 1995. Excluding capital gains on ship sales, profit fell by 48 million guilders.
Shipping tariffs slid by 11 percent through the year.
European Transport and Distribution results rose modestly to 52 million guilders from 47 million.

But Berndsen said the five million guilder gain did not reflect the division's improvement, notably in Germany, as last year's figure for Austrian operations had been inflated by 11 million guilders by a variety of factors.
"The real improvement is therefore 16 million (guilders)," he said.
Results from the Nedrill unit, sold on July 1 to Noble Drilling Corp of the United States, and other activities fell to 27 million guilders from 34 million.
Nedlloyd made clear it is pinning hopes on the merger of its container shipping operations with those of Peninsula and Oriental Steam Navigation Company last year.
Cost savings of $200 million are expected within 18 months.
Nedlloyd said its merger would make it one of the strongest in the ocean shipping industry, but it was too early to make a forecast for the joint venture.
"The platform is ready and it is encouraging for the future. We can manage our cost savings and we will sit much better with them," said Paul Bijvoets, executive board member of P&O Nedlloyd.
Nevertheless shipping rates would continue to decline.
For the company as a whole, Berndsen said Nedlloyd was on track to achieve its 10 percent return on capital employed target.
However, he declined to say when that target would be reached. In 1996, the return was between three and four percent, he said.
Analysts said the results were broadly in line with expectations, but they were mixed about Nedlloyd's prospects, notably in ocean shipping.
"The European Transport and Distribution division performed well in 1996 and prospects for 1997 are good. The merger with P&O seems to be working out," said Gert Jochems of NIB Securities.

"The fact they did not give a clear profit outlook for 1997 is interesting. The prospects for P&O Nedlloyd are not bright. There's an enormous need to limit costs and 1997 will be a difficult year in container shipping," said Henri Jongschaap at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.
($ = 1.897 Dutch Guilders)
